title: Approved after the fact, as an emergency, or without competition
question: How often do these boards approve a contract after the work started, or one that was never competed?
finding: The school board’s agendas carry 84 items that call a contract “retroactive” (work begun before approval), besides 123 routine batch ratifications; BART’s board was asked to approve 54 sole- or single-source purchases worth $1.60 billion as read; the bridge district ratified 19 emergency actions by its general manager worth $12.9 million.
how: Item text is searched for set phrases: "retroactive", "ratifies the emergency action", "sole source", "single source", "without competitive bid". Union contract ratifications and appointments are left out. The table includes every qualifying non-routine item, ordered by disclosed amount.
limits: These are board agenda items and resolutions: a ceiling the board was asked to authorise, not a payment, and the dollar figure is the first one a parser found in the text. An item on an agenda may have been amended or withdrawn. Each body is legally separate from the City. On the three routes: State law lets a general manager act in an emergency and report afterwards, a single-source purchase of parts for existing trains may have no real competitor (BART’s need a two-thirds vote), and a school site signing late is a paperwork failure more often than anything else. BART’s total is dominated by one 2018 authorisation to negotiate for more rail cars. Counts depend on how each body words its agenda.
